tier_reason: These are the project's own numbers from the README Benchmarks tables (fasthex 0.78s vs xxd 43.62s, hexyl and hexdump). The gist gives only the hardware, OS settings and 'Hyperfine, 3 warmup runs'. There is no published benchmark script, and no Rust version, build flags or tool versions. With flags unstated and gains over 50x, the tier is capped at C.

corrections.stars_or_usage: 13 stars; crates.io crate fasthex has 451 downloads (latest 0.3.28); README also lists AUR packages fasthex / fasthex-bin
corrections.caveats: The recorded benchmark_url (a gist) holds only the testing conditions: hardware, iommu settings and 'Hyperfine with 3 warmup runs'. The timing tables are in the README. No benchmark script is published, and no Rust version, build flags or xxd/hexyl/hexdump versions are given. Hardware is stated as 'Intel i5-7700T', which is not a real Intel SKU (i5-7600T and i7-7700T exist), so the CPU model is doubtful. The gains over 50x are not a like-for-like encoder comparison. fasthex formats in parallel with rayon over 64 MiB mmap chunks, uses AVX2/SSE4.1 SIMD, and writes zero-copy through vmsplice/splice, which makes output to /dev/null nearly free. xxd, hexyl and hexdump are single-threaded formatters. The tier is capped at C under the >50x unstated-flags rule.

notes: The README numbers match claimed_speedup exactly, including the 69 GiB result (fasthex ~1m vs hexyl ~1h 30m). benchmark_url now points to the README Benchmarks section because the gist has no numbers. tier_reason: The README performance section shows first-party timings of the native SSE4.2 CRC-32C against the addon's own table-based (slice-by-8) CRC-32C. The benchmark code is public (benchmark/*.js), but the compiler and optimisation level are unstated and the CPU is given only as 'Intel Core i7' on a MacBook Air. That is not A, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Native SSE4.2 CRC-32C vs native table-based CRC-32C: 4.319142 ms vs 10.726345 ms for 10000 iterations over a fixed buffer (~2.5x, derived from page data); 60.194043 ms vs 225.459861 ms over 10000 random-length buffers (~3.7x, derived from page data)
corrections.workload: Node.js native-addon benchmark (benchmark/single_fixed_size_buffer.benchmark.js and benchmark/multiple_random_size_buffers.benchmark.js): CRC-32C over a single fixed 1024-byte text buffer and over 10000 random-length buffers of 0-65535 bytes, 10000 iterations each
corrections.compiler_and_flags: node-gyp Release build; the SSE4.2 unit is compiled with -msse4.2 (binding.gyp); compiler and optimisation level are not stated
corrections.stars_or_usage: 133 stars; npm package sse4_crc32 had ~952k downloads in the last month (2026-08-27 to 2026-09-25)
corrections.caveats: The current README numbers date from the 2018-05-29 README/benchmark rewrite (commit 304ac875), not 2013; the 2013 and 2016 README versions showed different numbers and 8GB RAM. No compiler or optimisation level is stated, and the CPU is given only as 'Intel Core i7'. The baseline is the project's own table-based fallback (Mark Adler's slice-by-8 code) inside the same addon, not zlib crc32() or another external library. Timings include Node N-API call overhead on small buffers. The implementation is C++ (src/*.cpp), not C. The last commit on master is 2022-03-27 (the 2023-07-08 push date comes from a branch), so the repo is abandoned (>3 years). The Voxer/sse4_crc32 fork was created 2020-02-26, not 2019.

notes: The numbers match the README exactly. The ratios were not stated on the page, so they are now marked as derived.
